claims.text: The initial lightweight high-entropy alloy has a density below 6 g/cm^3.
The intervention is addition of 0.1–0.5 wt% boron.
The alloy is to be processed by mechanical alloying followed by spark plasma sintering.
Boron is to be introduced as elemental boron powder.
Boron addition will produce a boron-rich grain-boundary phase.
The boron-rich grain-boundary phase will enhance grain-boundary cohesion.
The boron-rich grain-boundary phase will reduce corrosion susceptibility.
The boron-rich grain-boundary phase will reduce oxidation susceptibility.
Boron atoms will segregate to grain boundaries.
Segregated boron will form a thin, stable boride phase at grain boundaries.
The grain-boundary boride phase will inhibit grain-boundary sliding.
Boron modification will increase room-temperature yield strength relative to the unmodified alloy.
Boron modification will increase room-temperature ultimate tensile strength relative to the unmodified alloy.
Boron modification will increase room-temperature elongation relative to the unmodified alloy.
Boron modification will improve saltwater corrosion resistance relative to the unmodified alloy.
Boron modification will improve high-temperature oxidation resistance in air relative to the unmodified alloy.
The boron-modified alloy will retain a density below 6 g/cm^3.
The boron addition must not exceed 0.5 wt%.
The optimal boron concentration is uncertain.
The precise mechanism by which boron affects the alloy properties is uncertain.

contradictions.description: The baseline is described as having the same composition as the modified alloy, but adding 0.1–0.5 wt% boron necessarily changes composition unless 'same composition' means the same base composition apart from boron.

The predicted outcome asserts improvement in all five measured properties, whereas the falsification rule allows the hypothesis to survive when only two properties improve by more than 10%, even if the remaining predicted properties do not improve or worsen.
